author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: IEC declares 2026 local elections free and fair as coalitions get set to run municipalities
content:
The Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) has declared the 2026 local government elections free and fair, with 14.9-million people having cast their ballots in an election that has left most municipal councils facing the prospect of coalition government.




The African National Congress (ANC) retained its position as the largest party nationally, securing 30.76% of the vote and 3,246 council seats. However, the result represents a significant decline in its electoral support and leaves the party needing to negotiate with other political formations in municipalities where it failed to secure an outright majority.




Announcing the results at the IEC results operations centre at Gallagher Estate on Sunday, IEC chairperson Mosotho Moepya said the elections had largely been conducted in a peaceful environment.




A total of 29.2-million voters were registered, with approximately 14.9-million participating. The national turnout was 52%, an increase of 6.1 percentage points from the 45.9% recorded in the 2021 local government elections.




The Democratic Alliance (DA) came second with 24.64% and 1,695 council seats, followed by the uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) with 9.76% and 785 seats. The Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) received 6.22% and 588 seats, while ActionSA secured 5.67% and 313 seats.

author: Anele Mbi
title: Polls close and the counting of votes has begun
content:
The Western Cape electoral officer, Michael Hendrickse told reporters that there were more people who voted in this year’s local government elections compared the previous poll in 2021. By 18h00, over 1.5 million people had voted. “Its clear that the number of voters is going upwards and will surpass the number of voters in the local government elections in 2021. But, there were fewer registered people in 2021 compared to this year. So, I’m not comparing the turnout as a proportion but looking at the numbers of people who voted,” he said.




Hendrickse said that there were still people waiting to vote at around 21h45 as they were in the queue by 21h00.




In Cape Town




Elitsha

 

reported earlier

 that voters in Khayelitsha and Mitchells Plain said that youth unemployment and lack of basic services are some of the issues that the next council should prioritise. Zine Malusi from ward 89 in Khayelitsha pleaded with political parties to work together to improve the lives of the poor even if they end up in coalition governments.




Her views were echoed by Fiona Jacobs from Portlands who said there was a need for the media to play an educational role in the elections to make sure that voters are clear who to vote for.




In Johannesburg




In Alexandra, unemployment and poor municipal services featured prominently in the concerns of young voters.




Bonang Makola, a first-time voter, said unemployment and the deteriorating state of Johannesburg influenced her decision at the ballot box. She had followed interviews in which political parties outlined their plans to reduce unemployment over the next five years, and their proposals helped shape her choice.




“As a young person, unemployment is one of the biggest issues. Some parties said they would reduce it by 0%, while others said they would reduce it by 2% every year. That influenced my decision on which party to vote for,” she said.




Makola said residents in her community continue to experience electricity problems, water interruptions and poor refuse collection. The accumulation of rubbish in Alexandra, she added, had become a serious health concern.




Thato Couch, a resident of Tsutsumani in Alexandra and a first-time voter, believes that the growing dissatisfaction with political parties has contributed to voter apathy. She said some residents no longer saw the point of voting because they felt that elections had brought little improvement to their circumstances. “People choose not to vote because they think it’s useless. There’s no change, no progress and nothing is actually moving. We just keep voting for the same thing,” she said.




Municipal workers fixing a blocked drain outside ward 89 voting station in Khayelitsha

.




Meanwhile, Rene, a Sandton resident, said Johannesburg’s deteriorating infrastructure requires urgent intervention, regardless of whether the next administration was formed by a single party or a coalition. She supports coalition governments provided political parties cooperate and share a commitment to fighting corruption and improving service delivery. “Johannesburg is falling apart. There has to be a party, whether it’s a coalition or a single party, that fixes this wonderful city because it’s broken through neglect,” she said.




Rene argued that political disagreements and leadership disputes should never take precedence over residents’ basic needs. “We’re the people. We pay our taxes and rates, yet our streets are full of potholes, we have no water, no electricity and the garbage isn’t being collected,” she said.




She also highlighted the dangers posed by poorly maintained roads, particularly for elderly motorists navigating streets without adequate lighting and road markings.




Across the interviews, voters expressed different perspectives on political parties and coalition government but shared a common expectation: those elected must demonstrate accountability and deliver tangible improvements. For Johannesburg residents, the real test of the elections will not simply be who wins political power, but whether that power translates into jobs, functioning infrastructure and reliable basic services.




In KuGompo City




Mdantsane residents, in Buffalo City Metropolitan Municipality, said that youth unemployment and service delivery should be one of the key things that the next council should focus on. 




According to Nosiseko Adonisi (79) who voted at Zanokukhunya Primary in Ward 20, the next local government should prioritise young people in terms of job creation and skills development. “There must be job creation for young people, and the government must assist them to get skills. We want a total change. Our lives must not be the same,” Adonisi said.




“Our roads are full of potholes, forcing cars to dodge. We also want officials to assist us properly when we visit government offices,” she added.




Ayanda Maphongolo said the first problem the new government must attend to is the roads. “We always must fix tires. It is no longer potholes, but we call them graveyards. Whoever is gonna come must make us happy as citizens. The new government must be able to fix all the problems we encounter at BCM.




“I don’t know why I have voted because there is no benefit from voting. There is no change and there won’t be change no matter who wins because they give jobs to themselves. Not all of us are able to be ANC volunteers I get employed. Look now I am busy selling chicken feet on the road and I don’t have time to volunteer.  We have nothing, no houses and no jobs but I have just voted for the sake of voting,” said Thotyelwa Halutyana.




Neliswa Nomji, a pensioner who stays in Cuba informal settlement, which is part of ward 14, felt that political parties need to meet with people first to decide which parties to go into coalition with. “Political parties must meet with the people first. They cannot just choose who to form coalition with on their own. They must meet with the people”,Nomji said.

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Slow start to elections in the Western Cape
content:
Voting started slowly in the Western Cape’s most populous townships, Mitchells Plain and Khayelitsha, today. When 

Elitsha

 visited voting stations in wards 96, 93 and 89 in Khayelitsha and 116 in Mitchells Plain, between 09h00 and 11h30, there were no queues and voters would arrive in groups, get processed and leave soon after.




According to the provincial electoral officer, Michael Hendrickse, all the Western Cape’s 1,623 voting stations were opened this morning but not without any hiccups. Problems with the voter management devices at some voting stations were resolved, while Hendrickse said, long queues at some voting stations were shortened by getting more personnel and material to the stations.




Hendrickse told reporters that by midday, the Independent Electoral Commission had issued just a quarter of all ballots, most of them in the City of Cape Town. 3.4 million registered voters in the Western Cape are expected to cast their votes today.




“At around 12h30 this afternoon, 824,242 voters were already issued with ballots in the province and of these, 524,162 were issued in the Cape Town Metro,” he said. He stressed that if a voter is in a queue by 21h00, they would still be able to vote.

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Western Cape police guard voting stations and taxi routes
content:
About 22,000 integrated law enforcement agencies including the police, law enforcement, defence force and traffic services have been deployed to 1,579 voting stations across the Western Cape. This was announced at the operational briefing in the early hours today by the provincial police commissioner, Lieutenant General Sizakhele Dyantyi. The police, according to Dyantyi, have categorised high-, medium- and low-risk voting stations and would be deployed in alignment with these identified needs. 




A police intelligence team has further identified 33 high-risk areas in the province based on previous incidents in these areas. “It is based on crime incidents that previously took place within those particular environments that lead to the conclusion to say this particular area and this particular voting station would be then high risk,” he said.




Dyantyi dispelled rumours that a shooting incident happened at a voting station in Manenberg yesterday. “It was as a response of the members of SAPS as they were doing their patrols, where they spotted a wanted suspect and when he noticed that the police had seen him, he pulled a firearm and the police responded. So, the incident was about the response of the police.

author: Anele Mbi
title: Buffalo City’s broken houses and decades of empty promises
content:
A housing rectification project in Braelyn Extension 10 in Buffalo City Municipality (BCM) has left residents frustrated with the municipality’s failure to address severe structural faults.




Serious defects in the RD houses include cracked walls and roofs, leaking roofs, and inadequate foundations. Braelyn residents say they have repeatedly complained to the municipality, which has promised to rebuild the houses since 2004, but has taken no action until today, except for a laydown yard constructed by the sitting, ANC ward councillor, Mendi Wetsetse.




The stalled housing project intersects with service-delivery defects across the ward, including unpaved and potholed roads, poor refuse collection, and electricity shortages brought about by the growing Inkandla informal settlement.




Recently, President Cyril Ramaphosa authorised the Special Investigating Unit (SIU) to probe allegations of extensive corruption and maladministration of major BCM tenders.




According to Braelyn residents, talks about rectifying Braelyn Ext 10 RDP houses began before 2010. The then ward councillor, Thabo Myira, who served as a councillor between 2005 and 2010, confirmed the claim.




Media reports also indicate that in 2009, the then minister of human settlements, Tokyo Sexwale promised people living in faulty RDP houses in East London that their houses would be rebuilt. Today, councillor Wetsetse, who is campaigning for a third term in the upcoming local government election, promised to rectify the situation.




Housing defects




Ntombizanele Mabala, an 80-year-old pensioner, said since residents arrived in Braelyn in 1997, they have complained to councillors and the municipality about the poor condition of their houses, but their pleas were ignored. “These are not houses but hokkies. We have children and a family of six. Rain comes in from every direction – through the roof, the walls and underneath – because these houses have no foundations,” she said. “The councillor promised that the housing rectification process would begin before 4 November, but there are still no signs of work apart from a laydown-yard fence erected two years ago.”




Another pensioner, Nothembile Mqhayi, whose house was built below ground level, said her house floods when it rains. She showed 

Elitsha

 a hole she had made at the bottom of a wall to let water that entered the house drain out.




The Mqhayi family had to make a hole in the wall to drain out water when the house floods.




Ziyanda Mpakantsho (42), who recently joined an EPWP project and earns R3,000 a month, said rectification is urgently needed because she lives with a sick and disabled person. “I grew up hearing that the cracks in the walls would be repaired, but many years have passed. These Braelyn houses have no proper foundations, so water leaks in when it rains. The houses have not been rectified because the money is being squandered,” she said.




Zama Thutha (70) said the government had not fixed the RDP houses because it was corrupt and unaccountable to voters. “Even the EPWP jobs created recently will end after the elections. Our system of government is capitalism, which puts profit before the needs of ordinary people,” he said.




Recurring delays and more promises




Responses from both the BCM and the Eastern Cape department of human settlements (DHS) are not only conflicting but also suggest the rectification process remains a false hope for Braelyn residents. When asked whether the municipality or its ward councillor has made any promises of rectification, the municipality said the provincial government is responsible for the rectification process.




“The Buffalo City Metropolitan Municipality wishes to clarify that it does not currently run a municipal housing rectification programme; this falls outside local government funding allocations. What we can say is that the laydown yard established on-site remains a site-securing measure for future development once capital is allocated.”




The laydown yard is overgrown

.




The provincial DHS said that, despite the constitutional principle of cooperative governance that compels the various spheres of government to share information and support each other, implementation requires compliance with the necessary technical, administrative, planning, and budgetary processes. The department has not denied the fact that rectification has been recognised for several years.




“The programme, which focuses on the rectification of existing two-room RDP houses, was prioritised following engagements involving the current ward councillor and the executive mayor of BCMM,” said Yanga Funani, the DHS spokesperson.




“In the current financial year, Braelyn, Ducats and Dimbaza have been identified among the priority areas for rectification,” said Funani. “The project is currently at an advanced preparatory stage, with implementation targeted to commence in November 2026, subject to the completion of outstanding administrative and implementation requirements,” he added.

author: Simon Ramapuputla
title: Cosatu to campaign for ANC and SACP
content:
Cosatu has pledged to campaign for both the African National Congress (ANC) and the South African Communist Party (SACP) in the upcoming local government elections, warning that its political support will not prevent it from confronting either party if workers’ interests are undermined.




SACP candidates will be contesting the local government polls on 4 November, independently of the ANC for the first time since 1994. 




The position emerged from the federation’s 15

th

 national congress, which was held from 12 to 14 October after its 

first attempt in September collapsed

. In her first formal press statement as the newly elected general secretary, Zingiswa Losi said the congress reaffirmed Cosatu’s historic mission to organise and mobilise the working class, defend workers’ rights and advance a programme of democratic transformation towards socialism.




The federation’s decision to support both the ANC and SACP followed consultations among affiliates. Losi explained that the unions had adopted positions intended to influence the national congress, which ultimately passed what the leadership called a “super resolution” to support both parties.

author: Ndivhuwo Mukwevho
title: Multi-million rand sports facility finally opens in Limpopo
content:
Finally, Waterval residents in Limpopo outside of Elim Hospital are now able to utilise their R55-million sports facility having waited for over a decade of delays. The Waterval facility is not the only one that has been neglected by Limpopo municipalities. Earlier this year, 

Elitsha 

reported on the R1.4-million upgrades to 

Makwarela Stadium

 that never happened.




How it all started




The Waterval sports facility, which consists of a soccer field and a tennis court, was officially handed over to the Waterval community earlier this month. This came as welcome relief to local residents who had already lost hope that the facility would ever open. At one stage, it was left abandoned and turned into a drug den and a hiding place for criminals.




The facility is set to be utilised for various sporting codes by the local communities and schools. “At last, our children have got a ground where they can play their football with ease. Even though we had to wait for years for the facility to be completed, we are happy now that the ground is ours. To be honest, I am one of the people who had already lost hope that one day, the facility will ever be used for our benefit,” says Cedric Mulaudzi, a resident of Waterval.

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Austerity under fire as Godongwana pauses fuel levies and low-cost housing
content:
Residents, activists, members of trade unions and civil society groups took to the streets of Cape Town earlier today against budget cuts. This was before the Medium Term Budget Policy Statement was delivered by the Minister of Finance, Enoch Godongwana. Led by Cry of the Xcluded, some of the protesters’ demands included the right to decent work, an end to exclusionary access to free basic services, an end to privatisation, an increase in health, education and policing, and an universal basic income amongst others.




Equal Education’s secretary general, Itumeleng Mothlabane said that the budget cuts in education have resulted in the existence of plain pit latrines in schools, overcrowded classrooms and learners having to walk on dangerous roads when they go to school.




“We reject a budget that continues to deprioritise the education of a poor black learner. We demand an increase in the allocation that is given to each and every learner. We demand an increase in the school infrastructure budget in Limpopo, KwaZulu-Natal, the Eastern Cape and all the rural provinces,” Mothlabane said.

author: Mzi Velapi
title: ‘End hunger, stop climate harm’: protesters take demands to Parliament
content:
About 200 residents and activists marched through the streets of Cape Town on World Food Day, calling for the government to end hunger and stop climate harm. Organised by the Climate Justice Charter Movement (CJCM) and the South African Food Sovereignty Campaign and allied partners, the protesters handed the memorandum to parliament where they called for the adoption of the People’s Sovereignty Act No 1 of 2024, a People’s Sovereignty Policy and an immediate ban on pesticides.




At least 14 to 15 million people in South Africa live below the food poverty line and experience regular food insecurity, while 11,000 children die due to malnutrition every year, and 10-million tonnes of food go to waste every year, according to Unite Against Hunger. 




A recent report by the International Panel of Experts on Sustainable Food Systems (IPES-Food) found that nearly 1.4-billion people in the world work in the agrifood sector, including farmworkers. Despite their number and the vital role they play, they are among the most exploited workers in the world.
